s10.slug: SATURDAY · 11:25 AM · JUSTIN HERMAN PLAZA, THE EMBARCADERO — THE RALLY
body: Peter finds a garage off Washington Street on the second try, and by the time the fourteen of them have walked back up to the plaza the crowd runs from the foot of the Ferry Building clock to the far side of the fountain and up the steps of the hotel. Thirty-five thousand, they’re saying. Gulls work the edges for dropped bagels. The wind comes straight off the Bay, wet and smelling of the ferries’ diesel, and finds every gap in the Carhartt.

It isn’t the crowd he had in his head. It’s young — college sweatshirts from schools he’s heard of and schools he hasn’t, a high school in matching green scarves, a little girl asleep on her father’s shoulders with her sign upside down in her fist, a row of nuns in gray habits and running shoes — and there are more women in it than anybody in the van expected. Margot has her notebook open against the wind. She writes that down.

The speakers are on a stage too far off to see. What reaches the back of the plaza is the loudspeakers, every sentence arriving twice, once from the stage and once off the face of the Hyatt: a young woman who runs some kind of organization, fast and sure of herself; then a woman from Texas who ran an abortion clinic until the fall and walked out of it. The crowd goes quiet for her in a way it hasn’t for anyone else, and then very loud. Jack gets what she says in pieces. He gets the applause whole. Somewhere behind the stage a choir is singing in Latin, a little behind itself.

Skye comes across the plaza while the woman from Texas is still talking, threading through the signs with a cardboard tray of two coffees held up over her head. Black beanie, sunglasses, jeans, and his flannel, buttoned to the throat, the cuffs turned back twice so her hands can get out. Over at the Newman banner, Lena’s eyes go to the flannel and away, down to her clipboard.

“I left at six,” Skye says, and puts a coffee in his hand. “I stopped in Gilroy, because I’d heard of it, and the coffee was garlic. Everything in Gilroy is garlic. I think they pump it in.” She turns in a slow circle, taking it in: the signs, the nuns, the sleeping girl, the gulls. “It’s like a Lakers parade where everyone’s sad.”
“It’s a funeral that’s hopeful.”
She looks at him over the sunglasses. “That’s better than mine,” she says. “I hate that.”
On the loudspeakers the woman from Texas is talking about the day she quit. Skye tips her head at the stage. “Who’s that?”
“She ran the clinic down there. Until October.”

“And now she’s here.” Skye listens to the rest of it with the coffee forgotten under her chin, and when the plaza goes loud for the woman she doesn’t clap, and doesn’t make a joke either. She keeps listening until it’s over.

Becca gets to her first, out of the Newman knot with her scarf wound twice and her arms already open, and hugs her, coffee and all, hard enough to bring her up onto her toes. “Your letter came on St. Agnes,” Becca says into the beanie. “I’m keeping it.”
“It was mostly a surfboard,” Skye says, muffled.
“The surfboard was good.” Becca lets her go. “You got the fins right. Most people don’t.”

The Dominguez brothers come through the crowd from the Market Street side in a wedge of red caps — Javi, Luis, Nico and Tito, up from San Jose, every one of them older than Clare and built along the general lines of a door — and Kevin, who has been preparing for this since Paso Robles, says hello to all four of them in a single breath, gives his name, his major, his parish, his GPA and his position on the 49ers’ offensive line, and runs out of air.

Skye hands Jack her coffee. She steps into the middle of them and gets their names one at a time, a handshake each, saying every name back as if she’s going to be tested on it, and then she lines them up by height, out loud, in the middle of the Walk for Life. “Javi, Nico, Luis — no. Tito, stand up straight. Javi, Tito, Nico, Luis.” Tito, who is twenty-one and hasn’t said a word yet, stands up straight. She turns to the eldest. “Javi. Joe Montana. Good Catholic? Because I have a feeling.”

Javi takes his cap off. “Notre Dame,” he says, with reverence, and after that the four of them are hers: Luis is doing the Catch with his hands, and Nico is correcting him, and Tito has begun, in a low voice, to talk.

Kevin stands beside Jack in his gloves, set free. That was supposed to be Jack’s job today — the extra man, the one who takes the brothers’ questions so Kevin doesn’t have to answer all of them at once. It’s what he came for. Kevin watches her do it in his place, and his ears go red to the tips, and he doesn’t say a word.
Margot hasn’t looked up from the notebook. Skye nods at it. “What are you studying?”
“Everyone,” says Margot, and turns the page.

Tyler and Kenzie hover at the edge of it, starstruck in the Newman way. Tyler gives her a pamphlet and a holy card of St. Gianna and tells her he’s glad she came, shining with it. Kenzie says, “I *knew* it was you at the Haiti table, I told everybody,” and holds her BlackBerry against her chest in both hands. Skye thanks Tyler and tucks the holy card into the flannel’s pocket, and asks Kenzie what she sings.
When the brothers have been handled, Lena comes over from the banner. People move for the clipboard. She stops in front of Skye and puts out her hand.
“You came,” Lena says. “You’re welcome here.”
Skye takes the hand. “I wanted to see.”
Lena nods. At the banner Peter is holding up one of the poles and calling her name, and she’s needed there.

Skye drinks her coffee. Over the lid her eyes go to the banner and come back to him — one look, not a long one — and he sees it, and she sees him see it. He hasn’t looked at the banner once. She smiles and holds the garlic coffee under his nose, and he declines it.

Two rows over, a girl in a Marquette sweatshirt lifts a phone. Skye’s smile starts — he sees it start, the bright practiced thing coming up into her face by itself, the way a knee comes up for the doctor’s hammer — and stops halfway. She pulls the beanie down to her eyebrows, turns her back on the phone and puts her face in his shoulder as if she’s cold. It isn’t her day. Jack moves half a step to the left, so that the girl in the Marquette sweatshirt gets a very good picture of the back of a Carhartt.

At ten past twelve the loudspeakers say something about the route that nobody at the back can make out, and the front of the crowd begins to move, and then the middle. The Newman banner comes up off the pavement on its two poles. Somebody behind them starts the rosary.

journal.title: Becca Lindell
journal.text: Coeur d’Alene. Seven siblings; wants seven or nine kids, odd numbers, for the tiebreaker. Can butcher a deer — elk too. Has pulled a calf, and it shows. Ran the beach cleanup like a cattle drive and put me on her team. Asked about the scar in the water. Told her mother the cleanup was a date, then asked me if it was. Wrote FRIDAY? on her clipboard, and meant it. Drives her brother Eli’s red Ranger; St. Isidore on the visor. Second date: Friday-night football. Knows downs. Prayed a Glory Be on fourth and one. Learned the First Way on the bleachers and said it back perfectly. Kissed my cheek so there’s no confusion. Third date was mine. I asked. I paid. The elephant seals at Piedras Blancas at sunset, in Kevin’s Odyssey. She knew what every one of them weighed. Nobody’s ever planned a thing for her, she says. She’s been praying for two in the morning. Named a hermit crab Thomas, after the First Way, and asked Fr. Osei whose blessing it was. Works the Marine Lab touch tank Thursday afternoons and Friday at six in the morning — that’s how she signed Thomas out. He’s home; she knows him by the chip in his shell. Mailed Rosie a birthday card with Thomas on it and six true facts on the back, to the address I gave her for her Christmas cards. She does them in October. Has a page on her clipboard for Wes. She’s been praying for him and Lena since September. Her eyes are gray. Brought a survival bag to the library for my midterm, with a clementine for Lena. Prays at two, like always. Took me to *Where the Wild Things Are* at the Rialto; her favorite line is the last one. My mother wrote her a thank-you note. Her list for Halloween says WE SHOULD MATCH!! It’s due Halloween. She says I look at her like homework. She says she’ll wait. Stuck on the touch tank all weekend while we were at Big Sur: the weekend volunteer has the swine flu. Asked me for the monks’ fruitcake for her Grandma Agnes — the only honest fruitcake in America. I handed in my homework six days early. St. Isidore and St. Maria: her first. Early, she said. Nobody’s early but her. Halloween: she sewed my costume out of a Rathdrum Feed & Seed sack. She was St. Maria de la Cabeza in Mrs. Fitch’s lace, with a water jug. Best Saint, by acclamation — a gold halo. Never won anything that wasn’t a heifer. Home at 11:40 for the six o’clock tank; the volunteer still has the flu. ‘Farmer.’ Theo’s birthday: huckleberry jam from her mother, for Theo — the Idaho gift. Next to his mother all night. ‘He’s *mine*. Since the beach cleanup.’ Toasted St. Martin de Porres: a dog and a cat and a mouse, one bowl. The Portolá steps, November 4th: her mom’s been calling me her boyfriend since September. She asked if she could tell her she’s right. I said yes. Her mom first, then Facebook. She flies home to Spokane the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Her mother has named the turkey. She asked how I’m getting home. Greyhound. She frowned. Her mother sent a box: socks, cookies, two jars of huckleberry — JACK, and FOR THE CATHOLIC ROOMMATE. She offered me Daisy’s money. Six hundred and twelve dollars. It’s there, she says. Daisy doesn’t mind. Saturday, Ohio State in overtime: she gave me a photograph of the elephant seals in a frame she painted, every seal labeled with what it weighs. She’ll call during her dad’s grace on Thanksgiving so I can hear it. She wants to watch Michigan here, with me. ‘Someday I want to see your house. Is that okay to say?’ Ma wrote her. Three days after Christmas. Pittsburgh’s cheaper than Cleveland. She looked. Wednesday, in Eli’s truck, I told her. She said she did everything right, and she did. ‘It just isn’t the thing, is it.’ She asked me to leave it up on Facebook till she’s told her mom at the table. Thursday at two she texted. Still praying for me — not a girlfriend thing, she says. At the twelve-ten she turned around across the aisle at the sign of peace and held out her hand. Then she held it out to Lena. At the airport, a week to the day: St. Raphael, for Nonna. Father Osei read the name at the twelve-ten, and she heard. Thanksgiving: told her mom at the table. Texted me first — happy Thanksgiving, praying for Nonna, taking it down now. Then she did. The Immaculate Conception, on the steps after the 12:10: white elephant, ten dollars, nothing that eats. Thomas is going home to Idaho in a Tupperware to see snow. The Advent party: ran the white elephant like a cattle auction. Three steals and it’s frozen. Her Christmas card found me in the lobby on finals Monday — six true facts about hermit crabs; number six, they need a friend. She sent my family one too, praying for Nonna’s hand, and Ma stood it at the front of the mantel. Christmas Eve she wrote on my Wall. The first day back, on the steps of St. Brendan’s, she said she saw, and she’s happy for me. Over Christmas she prayed I’d be happy. Thomas saw snow. At the Haiti table: her grandmother prayed that rosary at the gate of the Sunshine Mine in 1972, eight days. On the eighth day two men came up. She lent Skye her apron. Skye wrote her a letter, on paper. It came on St. Agnes, with a surfboard drawn on the back. At the Walk for Life she hugged Skye and told her she’s keeping the letter.

choices.text: *Walk her in with Newman. She’s with you.*
response: He takes her hand and walks her into the Newman crowd behind the banner — in among Becca and Tyler and Joey and the brothers, in front of every phone in the plaza, his hand around hers where anybody can see it. She lets herself be walked. Her fingers are cold and they hold on.
Peter, walking backward to count heads, hands her a sign off the stack without looking at who she is. She reads it, and looks up at Jack, and hands it to Tito, who is taller.
“She’s here for the anthropology,” Jack tells Tyler, who asked.
Margot, without looking up: “That’s mine.”

“We can share,” Skye says. “You take the women. I’ll take the men.” She hooks one arm through Javi’s and the other through Jack’s and steps off with one of them on each side, and Javi, who is twenty-seven, walks the first block like somebody who’s been asked to a dance.

choices.text: *Let her pick where she walks. She’s better at rooms.*
response: He doesn’t place her. He lets her look, and she looks over the moving crowd once, quick, reading it — where the phones are, where the cameras on poles are, where the light is — and picks: a few yards behind the Newman banner, beside Clare and the brothers, where four sets of shoulders in red caps stand between her and most of the plaza. She puts him on her other side.
“Good spot,” he says.
“Best in the house,” says Skye, and takes his arm.

s11.slug: SATURDAY · 12:10 PM · THE EMBARCADERO — “EXPLAIN IT WHILE WE WALK”
body: The Embarcadero opens out ahead of them, wide and flat and lined with palms — the Bay on the right with Alcatraz sitting out in it, Coit Tower up on its hill to the left — and the march fills it curb to curb and moves along it at the speed of the slowest stroller. The Newman banner is a few yards ahead: Peter on one pole and Lena on the other, two backs and a bedsheet of painted letters. Clare walks near the curb with her rosary, her lips going.
“You explain it while we walk,” Skye says. “That’s the rule.”
“We’re barely walking.”
“Then explain it slowly.” She tucks her arm through his. “Start where it starts. You always start where it starts.”

So he starts where it starts. That it’s somebody from the beginning — not a someday somebody, a somebody, small. That every line anybody has drawn after that point is somebody bigger deciding who counts, and the people who get to decide who counts have a long record, and most of it is terrible. That he didn’t get it off a pamphlet. He got it out of Aquinas and a biology textbook, in that order, and then in the other order, and they came out in the same place.

“Aquinas and a biology textbook,” Skye says. “My tutor would have wept.” She bumps him with her hip. “My turn.” She counts on the fingers of the hand that isn’t holding his arm. “Since I was twelve, my body has had a board of directors. My mother. Skylark. Wardrobe. The network. When I was fifteen, a man at the network I’d met twice sent a note about my weight, and my mother put it on the refrigerator under a magnet shaped like a strawberry, so I’d see it at breakfast. I have had my hair cut on a vote.” She is walking faster. “It is the one thing — the *one* thing — that’s mine to decide. And every girl should get to decide it. It isn’t a bumper sticker to me, Jack. It’s the only room in the building I have a key to.”

She’s walking faster with every sentence, faster than the march, nearly up on the heels of the family in front of them. He slows down. He walks at the speed of the stroller, on purpose, and because her arm is through his she has to slow down with him; after a few yards she does, and her voice comes down with her feet.

“It’s your body,” he says. “I’m not arguing about your body. I’d fight the network about your body. I’d fight your mother.” She snorts. “But the kid isn’t your body. It’s in it. It’s got its own heart going by six weeks, its own blood type. Half of it isn’t even yours. Here’s my whole argument: nobody gets to own anybody. Not a network. Not a mother. Not a man. That’s it. That’s the argument, and it’s yours too.”
He has got louder than he meant to, and a man in a Knights of Columbus jacket turns around to nod at him. Skye watches the man turn back.
“His family said he was out of his mind,” she says.
“That’s the Gospel for today.”
“I know. I read ahead. I always read ahead.” She pats his arm. “Fine. A philosopher.”

She had a tutor on set, she tells him, the year she was sixteen, because the State of California requires a minor on a soundstage to be educated between setups, and the tutor was a grad student from UCLA who was bored to death with algebra and gave her an essay by a woman at MIT instead. “You wake up in a hospital bed,” Skye says, “back to back with a famous violinist. He’s unconscious. He has a kidney thing, and you’re the only match, so the Society of Music Lovers kidnapped you in the night and plugged him into you. Nine months and he’s cured. Unplug, and he dies. Do you have to stay?” She lets a woman with a double stroller go by. “I read that in a trailer, in a school uniform from wardrobe, with a crew of sixty outside waiting for me to finish my homework so they could get paid. The famous one, kept alive on somebody else’s body. Believe me, I noticed. And I still think she’s right. You don’t have to stay plugged in. Nobody gets to make you.”

“The violinist’s a stranger,” Jack says. “You got kidnapped for him. It’s a great argument about strangers.” He looks up the road at the bedsheet letters and back at her. “A kid’s the one person on earth you didn’t have to be kidnapped to owe anything to. Your mother didn’t have to be kidnapped to owe you something. She owed you because she’s your —”
He hears it on the way out. It’s too late to get it back.

Skye looks at him. “Careful,” she says, mildly. And then she plays the harder card off the top of her own deck. “She built it for the worst case, you know. The kidnapping is the worst case. She says so.”

“I know.” He walks a few steps. “That’s the one I don’t have a speech for. I have the same answer, and I know what it costs somebody who isn’t me to hear it. I’m not going to pretend I know what it costs.”

She studies him, walking, and doesn’t push it; what she wanted, apparently, was to see whether he’d make a speech. “I’ve known girls who did it,” she says. “On sets. Sixteen. Nineteen. One of them was better than I’ll ever be. She drove herself, on a Friday, and on Monday she hit every mark and every line, and she wasn’t a monster, Jack. Some of them were sad about it. Some of them were glad.”

“I don’t think she’s a monster.” He means to stop there and doesn’t. “Dorothy Day had an abortion. Nineteen-nineteen; she was twenty-one. She wrote about it, and she grieved it as long as she lived, and she spent the rest of her life feeding people. If she’s a monster, I don’t know what the rest of us are.”
Skye looks at him sideways. “That’s your best one,” she says. “You saved it.”

They are passing a group of women walking together near the curb, older, forties and fifties, in parkas and sneakers, carrying signs that say what they did, and that they regret it. Some are hand-lettered and some are printed; there’s a year on one, a first name on another. Skye has walked past ten thousand slogans since the plaza without slowing down. She slows down here. She reads the nearest sign to the bottom, her lips moving a little, the way they move when she’s learning a line, and the woman carrying it — gray-blond, in a Giants scarf — nods to her, and Skye nods back, and for a while she doesn’t argue anything at all.
“They’re not saying it to me,” she says finally, low. “That’s what gets me. They’re not trying to win anything. They’re just — carrying it.”
A few yards off, walking with Clare’s brothers, Margot has stopped writing. She has the cap of her pen against her lip and her eyes on Skye, and she is listening.

When Skye starts again it’s quieter, and it’s the best thing she’s said all day. “Here’s what I’d tell this crowd if they gave me the stage. This is cheap. Thirty-five thousand people and a choir is cheap, if nobody pays for the girl at nineteen in a town like yours. Who pays her rent? Who drives her to the appointment, when the boyfriend’s gone to Akron and her mother won’t look at her across the table? The woman on the stage?” She stops walking, and a family with a wagon steers around them. “You?”

choices.text: “That’s your argument — nobody gets to own anybody. I’m just extending it.”
choices.key: On the Walk for Life you explained it while you walked. She didn’t agree, and she walked the whole way.
response: “That’s your argument,” Jack says. “That nobody gets to own anybody. I’m just extending it. To the kid.”
“That’s a good line,” Skye says, “and it’s a line.” She starts walking again. “I asked you who pays her rent.”

And she makes him answer it — not the kid, the girl — for the length of the next pier, and the one after it, while Alcatraz sits out in the Bay getting no closer. He does it badly. He has the parishes back home that pay a girl’s rent and don’t ask her name; he has the women from a pregnancy center who drive mothers to every appointment in their own cars; he has to admit there aren’t enough of either. She takes that one. She takes it in front of a Knight of Columbus who has been listening since the plaza, and the Knight nods at her.

choices.text: “You’re right that it’s cheap if nobody pays for the girl after.”
choices.key: On the Walk for Life you explained it while you walked. She didn’t agree, and she walked the whole way.
response: “You’re right,” Jack says. “It’s cheap if nobody pays for the girl after.”
She stands in the middle of the Embarcadero with her mouth open, and the march goes around them on both sides like water around a piling.
“Say it at the next pier,” she says.

He says it at the next pier. He adds what he has: the parishes back home that pay a girl’s rent and don’t ask her name, the women from a pregnancy center who drive mothers to every appointment in their own cars — and that there aren’t enough of them, nowhere near. She wins the girl at nineteen, outright, and he gives it to her. He keeps the kid. She lets him keep it, for now, the way you let somebody keep the last word when you’ve already got the trophy.

choices.text: “The girl at nineteen and the kid — I don’t think you get to pick one.”
choices.key: On the Walk for Life you explained it while you walked. She didn’t agree, and she walked the whole way.
response: “The girl at nineteen and the kid,” Jack says. “I don’t think you get to pick one. I think it’s both or you’re lying.”
“Then you’re going to lose a lot of arguments,” Skye says. “In this crowd too.”
“I know.”
She looks past him at the women with the signs, and then at the march going by, the sweatshirts and the nuns and the Knights, and back at him. “How many?”

He thinks about it honestly. He loses it at Newman about once a week — to Margot, to the guy who says the march is the work. He loses it at his own kitchen table. He walks anyway. He tells her so, and she wins that one: she makes him say, on the Embarcadero, that his own side doesn’t do both either, and she counts it.

choices.text: “You’ve been incorporated since twelve. The kid hasn’t even been incorporated.”
choices.key: On the Walk for Life you explained it while you walked. She didn’t agree, and she walked the whole way.
response: “You’ve been incorporated since twelve,” Jack says. “The kid hasn’t even been incorporated.”
Skye laughs out loud, in the middle of the Walk for Life, so suddenly that the Knight of Columbus turns around again.

And she makes him pay for it. She makes him pay for the next half mile — the long stretch past the piers, with the tourists at the rail of Pier 39 looking down at them — and she wins it. A corporation, she points out, at least gets a lawyer. A corporation has an accountant in Encino and a board and a mother who signs for it, and the girl at nineteen has a Greyhound schedule and a boyfriend who stopped answering, and if he’s going to make jokes about personhood he’d better be ready to hire her one. He isn’t. He says so. She takes the half mile.

s11a.slug: SATURDAY · 1:20 PM · THE EMBARCADERO, THE SIDEWALK — A MAN WITH A MEGAPHONE
body: Past the piers the sidewalk on the left belongs to the other side: a few dozen people, with a couple of bicycle cops leaning on their handlebars at the end of the block, and hand-lettered signs and a megaphone and a chant that rhymes rosaries with ovaries and has advice for the marchers about where to keep each.

The man with the megaphone is in his sixties — a gray ponytail, a fleece vest, a sign under his arm lettered on the back of a calendar page with a woman’s name and a year, DENISE · 1969, and nothing else. The year is from before Roe. He has been working the march for blocks, and the march has been letting him.

Then he sees Clare. She’s at the edge of the crowd by the curb with her rosary wound through her fingers, her lips moving, her eyes down, and he comes off the sidewalk at her with the megaphone a foot from her face and says things into it that are crude and close and built to hurt a nineteen-year-old girl, and the megaphone makes every one of them enormous.
Clare keeps praying. The beads go through her fingers at the same speed.
Skye lets go of Jack’s arm and steps in between them.
“She’s nineteen and she’s praying,” Skye says. “Yell at me. I’m on your side.”

The man stops. He looks at her — the beanie, the sunglasses, a man’s flannel buttoned to the throat — and he has no idea who she is; it isn’t anywhere in his face. After a moment he gets it, or gets a version of it, and he turns the megaphone on her. “Then what are you *doing* in there?” His voice cracks on the top of it. “You’re worse than they are. They don’t know any better. You know better and you walk with them anyway.”
The heat comes up the back of Jack’s neck and into his face, fast — the way it comes now only when somebody goes at her — and his hand closes on the cup.
Without looking around, Skye puts one hand back against his chest, and she leaves it there.
“Sir,” she says to the man, pleasantly, at the volume of a dinner party. “I’m agreeing with you. Agree back quieter.”

The sidewalk laughs — his own side, a woman with a wire coat hanger on her sign, a kid in a beret — and a few people on the march laugh with them. The man’s face goes dark red. He brings the megaphone back up.

Ahead at the banner Lena has turned around at the noise, the pole in both hands, and she is looking at Skye. A few yards behind them Kenzie has her BlackBerry up, and has had it up since the man came off the sidewalk.
And Jack is still lit, under Skye’s hand, with the megaphone coming back up a foot from her face.

journal.title: Clare Dominguez
journal.text: Clare Dominguez. Newman sophomore. Plays violin in the Mass band. Played ‘Ashokan Farewell’ at the Haiti table and people stopped on the lawn. Kevin’s mother knows her mother. Everybody’s mother knows her mother. Four brothers, back in San Jose. Knows football better than Kevin. Wore a 49ers cap to Sully’s. At the Walk for Life a man with a megaphone screamed at her, and she kept praying. Skye stood in front of her.

response: He steps up. He gets one step, and her hand stops him — closes on his shirt through the open jacket and holds, with more in it than he’d have guessed was in her arm.
“Down, Ohio,” she says, without turning around.

The man looks at Jack, all six feet of him, and at the girl holding him back by a fistful of shirt, and finishes what he had to say a good deal faster than he meant to, and returns to the curb with his calendar page.
A block on, her arm back through his and her eyes on the road, Skye says, “You were going to loom at a man at the Walk for Life.”
“I wasn’t going to do anything.”
“You were going to loom. Professionally. I felt it through the shirt.” She walks a few steps. “I’m not going to say anything about it now. I’m saving it for later. I have plans for it.”

choices.text: *Let her handle it. Stand where he can see you.*
response: He doesn’t step up. He stays exactly where he is, at her shoulder, close enough that she can feel him there, and lets the man look at him.

The man looks — up, at a kid from Youngstown in a work jacket who isn’t saying a word — and the rest of what he has comes out faster, and shorter, and more to the sidewalk than to her. The megaphone comes down. He turns away with the calendar page under his arm.

Skye keeps her hand where it is until the man is back on the curb. Only then does she take Jack’s arm again, and they walk on, and she doesn’t say anything for a block, and then she says, very fast, “You’re a very good wall. Ten out of ten.”
He holds out the coffee. It’s the one she brought him from Gilroy, two-thirds gone and stone cold.
“It’s cold,” Jack says, “and it tastes like garlic. You sound like you could use it.”

The sidewalk laughs again, harder, both sides of it. And the man, astonishingly — after he has looked at the cup, and at Jack, and at the girl with her hand on Jack’s chest — takes it. He doesn’t drink it. He carries it back to the sidewalk in one hand with the megaphone in the other, and stands there holding both, and Skye has to put her face in Jack’s sleeve to keep walking.

s12b.slug: SATURDAY · 2:50 PM · THE END OF THE ROUTE — THE SAAB, AT THE CURB
body: The Saab comes up the Embarcadero against the buses with its top up and its hazards going, twenty-five minutes after she left in a cab to fetch it, and double-parks beside the van. The signs are going into the back in stacks. Peter walks the length of the curb telling everybody “Ten past,” as if they might have forgotten.
His hands haven’t stopped shaking since the curb. He puts them in the pockets of the Carhartt so nobody has to see it.

Skye looks at Jack’s face through the windshield. She puts the car in park, gets out, comes around the long hood in his flannel with the hazards blinking orange on the both of them, and stands next to him on the curb with her shoulder against his arm, facing the way he’s facing, which is at nothing in particular. It’s what she does instead of asking.
Peter comes down the curb on his circuit, sees the Saab, sees Skye, and says “Ten past” to her too, politely, in case she’s coming.
“I’ll be ready,” Skye tells him, with a perfectly straight face, and Peter nods and moves on to Joey.

Kevin is in the van’s side door with the list against his chest and his pen uncapped. Behind him, through the open door, row three: the cooler in the aisle seat, Clare’s backpack of signs, the window and the middle.

Six hours either way. Six hours in a box with no door, with *Thank you for coming, Jack* sitting in the front of it, or six hours of the coast with the girl leaning on his arm. There isn’t a contest. There is Kevin, in a hall at half past eleven on Thursday in his pajama pants, asking him for something with an *I* in it.
“One second,” he tells Skye. She lets go of his arm.
He goes to the side door. “Kev. Can I ask you something, and you tell me the truth?”
“I always tell the truth. Margot says it’s a condition.”

“If I go back with Skye instead. Is that okay?” He keeps going before Kevin can be polite. “Because if you need me in the van the way you needed me to come up, I’ll get in the van. I mean it. I’ll sit on the cooler.”

Kevin looks at the list. He looks down the bench at Clare, who is in the second row with a rolled sign across her knees and her coat buttoned to the chin, talking to Becca. He looks at Jack’s face, and whatever is still on it from ten minutes ago, and Jack watches him take the question seriously, which is the only way Kevin knows how to take one.

“The brothers went home in Javi’s truck,” Kevin says. “Skye did the brothers. That was what I needed you for, and it’s done, and you didn’t even have to do it.” He clicks the pen. “So, the truth. I don’t need you. I’d like you. Six hours, and I’ve never sat next to a girl for six hours who wasn’t my sister, and I don’t know what I talk about at hour four. That’s the truth. But that’s mine. You came. That was the ask.” His ears have gone red to the tops. “Whichever. Really.”
It’s both halves, in order, the way Kevin gives the dosage and then the side effects. Jack heard both.

choices.text: *Hear the half he said second. Ride home with Kevin.*
choices.key: You asked Kevin if you could go home with Skye. He said he’d like you in the van, and you rode home in the van.
response: “I’m on the cooler,” he tells Kevin.
Kevin opens his mouth to argue, and shuts it, and makes a small mark on the list next to a name that was already checked.
Jack goes back to the curb. Skye has heard all of it from four feet away; she has a professional’s ears. She looks over at Kevin in the doorway with his list, and back.

“Go be Kevin’s,” she says. She kisses him on the curb, and gets in, and rolls the window down and pulls him down to it by the collar and kisses him again through it, quick. When she noses out into the traffic he can see her face through the glass — not hurt. Thinking. Thinking about his face, and what was on it, the thing she didn’t ask about.

choices.text: *Take him at his word. Go home with Skye.*
choices.key: You asked Kevin if you could go home with Skye. He told you the truth — he’d like you there, he didn’t need you — and you went with Skye.

journal.title: Kevin Tran
journal.text: Kevin Tran. Goes to daily Mass, saves you a seat with a Bible. Has a sister, Tina, in dental school, who flossed in the womb. Lies to his mom about orgo in Vietnamese. Drives his mother’s Odyssey at sixty-five, not sixty-six. His dad has two nail-salon supply stores in San Jose and has never had a Labor Day. Brought six pairs of gloves to a beach cleanup. Mouthed every word of Joey’s first reading from the second pew. Somebody coached Joey; I can guess who. Brought tea to a wake. His Bà Nội says heaven makes the elephant and heaven makes the grass. Walked Margot down at four in the morning. Handed Lena a roll of quarters for the payphone before she asked. Halloween: All Saints, every one nobody’s heard of — scrubs, a halo and a white mask. He found Laney. Friday night a pre-med said Maine got it right. Kevin answered him and went to get water. Tuesday, the Vietnamese Martyrs: his mother reads eleven of the hundred and seventeen. Asked about the scar. Alarm Five, on the lawn: he had a question mark next to my name on his clipboard. I told Priya I was out. He erased it. Tuesday at four I woke him for Doug. A chair under the knob, then a bell. Wednesday at the Brick, at the next carrel all night: ‘You two have been defending each other for three hours. That isn’t studying.’ Sings bass. A real one. Seven years of Vietnamese choir in San Jose — his mother made him. Friday, from the Odyssey: Go home. Sleep. Tell somebody something. Back from San Jose. His mother has a girl from their parish she wants him to call. Clare. She plays the violin in the Mass band. Wednesday he brought two flats of water to the Haiti table, which nobody asked for, and stayed to hold Clare’s violin case. ‘My mother knows your mother.’ Thursday he called Clare. His mother had the number, and his grandmother was on the speaker. She said yes to Sully’s. MLK Day he brought gloves for everybody. Tuesday in the basement he read us the first reading off his BlackBerry. Clare’s going to the Walk for Life, and so is he. He asked me to come — for him. I said yes. At the Walk he met all four of Clare’s brothers, and Skye took them off his hands. I asked if I could ride home with Skye. He said he didn’t need me, he’d like me — and that was his, not mine. Then he said go, and that he’d lie about it.

response: “Go,” Kevin says, while Jack is still looking for the first word. “I’ll lie about it.”

He would, and he’d be terrible at it; he’d tell Peter something so detailed that Peter would call Jack’s mother. He puts a line through Jack’s name, neatly, and beside it, in very small letters, writes *excused*.
Skye opens the passenger door from the curb side and holds it for him, like a driver at an airport, and Jack gets in.

s13s.slug: SATURDAY · 3:10–9:50 PM · US-101 SOUTH → PISMO BEACH, THE DUNES IN THE HEADLIGHTS
body: The Saab gets out of the city past the ballpark and up onto the freeway with the top up and the heater on their shins, and for the first twenty minutes nobody says anything, and it’s fine.
South of the airport, with a plane coming in so low over the freeway he can read the tail, the clock on the dash turns over to 3:30. Skye looks at it. She says nothing. He sees her say nothing.

The Peninsula goes by, and San Jose, and the long flat stretch where the orchards used to be. At Gilroy the garlic comes in through the vents again, and she doesn’t make the joke. Her right thumb has started on the steering wheel, back and forth along the stitched seam at the top of it. He looks out at the outlet mall and lets it get where it’s going.
“My mother called Friday,” Skye says. “At seven. With notes.”
He waits.

“The cold on the *s*. She could hear the honey, she said; she always can. And the boathouse — she wanted the first *safe*, not the second. *You’re safe, sweetie.* She’d have hit the first one.” The thumb goes along the seam. “She’s right. I hate that she’s right. And then the coat. She said the peacoat was doing a lot of work, and somebody ought to tell craft services they weren’t helping it, and then she laughed, so it was a joke.” A truck goes by them on the right, loud. “I put her on speaker in the shower. I set the phone on the back of the toilet and turned the water up as far as it goes, so the water would be louder than she was. I stood in there forty minutes and said *uh-huh* every time she stopped.”
The thumb stops.
“I’m nineteen,” she says, “and I hide from my mother in a shower.”
He leaves it the size it is.

She’s bright again almost at once, too fast. “Anyway. I was very good in that boathouse. I’m a very good scene partner. Ask anybody — I give, I take, I listen, I land the button.” She checks the mirror, changes lanes, changes back. “I’m afraid I’m only a very good scene partner.”
He thinks of the curb an hour ago: the Saab double-parked with its hazards going and her getting out of it, coming around the hood, standing next to him facing nothing.
“Scene partners stay in the car,” he says.

She looks over at him, fast, and back at the road, and something goes out of her shoulders. “That’s a good note,” she says. “I’m stealing it.” Then: “Your turn. I went first. That’s how it works — I go first, and then you have somewhere to put yours.”
There was a fight, he tells her. At the van, after she left for the car.
“About?”
“About you,” he says. “Sort of.”
He hears how small that is as soon as it’s out. She hears it too; her thumb doesn’t start again. There’s a name in the car and nobody says it.
“There’s more,” he says. “There’s Tuesday too. I’m going to tell you. Not in the dark at seventy, with you driving.”
She keeps her eyes on the road a long moment. “Daylight,” she says, the way she’d write it on a call sheet, and lets it be.

South of Salinas the light goes. The fields on both sides turn blue, and then there are only the long silver lines of the irrigation pipe holding on to the last of it, and then not even those. She reaches over without looking and thumbs through the iPod in the cupholder and puts something on — a guitar, two voices, low and close and hardly there — in place of the next question.

At King City she gets off for gas and goes in to buy, she announces, the worst snacks in the store, on principle. Under the canopy lights the RAZR, which has been in the Carhartt since the plaza, buzzes four times against his ribs.

body: She comes back out with a plastic bag — pork rinds, circus peanuts, a Big Hunk, a pickle in a pouch — and gets in, and he reads her the third one.
“What’s the Dell?”
“The computer. In the kitchen, by the phone.” He can see it. “She doesn’t sit down at it. She stands over it with her arms folded, like it might be catching.”
Skye doesn’t make a joke. She sits with the bag in her lap and the key in her hand, looking at the pumps. Then she starts the car.

By San Ardo she has recovered enough to present the snacks. She holds each one up into the dash light and scores it out of ten for badness — the pork rinds a solid six, the pickle an eight “for the pouch alone,” the Big Hunk a mystery she refuses to score until she’s chewed it for a full minute. He tells her circus peanuts are illegal in Ohio. She makes him eat one. It tastes like a banana that went to the dentist, and he says so, and she laughs so hard she drifts onto the rumble strip and back.

Somewhere past Paso Robles he tells her he’s going to meet the van at midnight at St. Brendan’s and help Kevin with the signs. He doesn’t tell her the other half of why. She says it’s very Catholic of him, and it comes out kind.

Past San Luis Obispo she takes the exit for the beach without a word. She goes down Grand Avenue to where the road runs out onto the sand — a ramp for trucks, a sign about the tide, nobody else — and stops at the foot of it with the headlights out across the dunes to the water, where the surf stands up white in the beams and falls over.

She cuts the engine and leaves the lights on. She’s out of her shoes and out of the car before he has his seat belt off, running down the sand into the headlights in her jeans and his flannel, and she doesn’t stop at the edge. She goes straight into the Pacific in January, to her knees, to her waist, and a wave stands up in the light and comes down on top of her, and she comes up out of it shrieking.
“*No people!*” she shouts back at him, arms out. “*There aren’t any people!*”

He goes in after her. The cold doesn’t feel like cold; it feels like being hit. It takes the breath out of him in one piece and his whole body locks up around his heart, and she’s laughing at him with her teeth going, and the next wave takes the two of them down together, and when he comes up he’s wet to the skin and past it, salt in his nose and his ears, and she has him by the front of the Carhartt and kisses him with her mouth cold and tasting of the sea. Up and down the beach, as far as the headlights go, there is nobody but them. He is laughing too.

Walking back up the sand to the car, dripping, her shoes in one hand and his wrist in the other, she says it again, quieter. “Thirty-five thousand people today. And nobody wanted anything from me. Not one.” She lets go of his wrist to push the wet hair off her face. “I didn’t know where to put my face. All day. I kept waiting for somebody to need it.”
He takes the shoes from her, so she has both hands for her hair.

Afterward they sit in the Saab with the doors shut and the heater on full and the headlights still out over the water, steaming like two pots on a stove. Her hair hangs in black strings. His jeans weigh forty pounds. She digs the white phone out of the glove box, where she left it safe, holds it out at arm’s length with the back toward them, leans her soaked head against his, and takes it. She turns it around to look: two drowned people in a car, lit green from below by the dashboard with the black windshield behind, her mouth open laughing and his eyes shut against her hair.

response: She looks at him to see if he means it. He does. She types with one thumb while her hair drips on the screen, deletes what she typed, and types something else.

response: She drives the rest of the way in her soaked jeans with the heater on high and the pork rinds open in his lap. At ten to ten she pulls up at the Delgado curb, both of them still faintly steaming. He gets the door open. She catches his sleeve.
“Change,” she says. “You smell like a pier.” And she lets go.
She looks at it a long time in the green light of the dash, the two drowned faces. At last she turns the phone over and lays it face down on the dashboard, carefully, a card she isn’t going to play.
“Mine,” she says.

It rides there face down up the Cuesta Grade and down the other side, and she doesn’t touch it once. At ten to ten, at the Delgado curb, she leans across him to get his door, which sticks, and says against his wet ear, “Go carry your signs.”
“*Field data*,” Skye repeats, enchanted, and types it with her thumb before he can take it back.

response: She wraps herself to the chin in the scratchy blanket from the trunk and drives home like that, steering through a gap in the wool, and reads him, from memory, everything she can remember about the temperature of the California Current from chapter four. At ten to ten she pulls up at the Delgado curb.
“Fenner’s going to want a lab report,” she says. “You write it. I was the sample.”
